title: I'm (Kind Of) Changing My Mind About Blue Books
author: Sydney Sharkey, PhD
summary: A writing instructor who long opposed Blue Books as an outdated, punitive assessment mode finds herself reconsidering—not to bring back handwritten exams but to reclaim what they represent: assessment centered on visible thinking rather than polished products. The arrival of generative AI has exposed a fundamental weakness in product-based assessment: a grammatically correct, well-organized document no longer provides meaningful evidence of student learning when AI tools can produce one in seconds. The productive question AI forces is not how to catch cheating but what evidence of learning we actually want to see. The author's proposed approach—asking students to identify and explain three deliberate rhetorical decisions embedded in any written piece—combines metacognitive reflection with retrieval practice, two of the most research-supported learning mechanisms. Critically, this approach works regardless of format: Blue Book, digital annotation, oral reflection, or recorded think-aloud. The deeper concern left unresolved is whether any assessment that emerges from AI anxiety can ever be genuinely pedagogical, or whether it remains surveillance rebranded with more appealing language.
points: AI has revealed the central limitation of product-based writing assessment: a polished document no longer provides evidence of learning when tools can generate grammatically correct prose, reorganize paragraphs, and imitate disciplinary conventions in seconds.

The productive question AI forces is not 'how do we prevent cheating?' but 'what evidence of learning do we actually want to see?'—a shift that reframes assessment from an integrity mechanism to a learning strategy.

Asking students to identify and explain three deliberate rhetorical decisions they made in a piece of writing combines two research-supported learning mechanisms: metacognitive reflection and retrieval practice, both of which deepen understanding beyond what producing a polished product demonstrates.

Visible thinking as an anti-cheating strategy and visible thinking as a learning strategy may use identical assignments—but the pedagogy is completely different, and the difference lies in the purpose behind the design.

The Blue Books debate is a proxy for a deeper question about the purpose of writing assessment: whether we are evaluating products or understanding the thinking that produced them—and AI has made ignoring that distinction impossible.
quotes: As a writing instructor, I have spent years arguing against the kinds of assessments they represent. Timed, handwritten exams have always felt disconnected from the way people actually write. Professional writing is iterative. We brainstorm, draft, revise, seek feedback, and rethink our ideas.

a polished document no longer tells me everything I want to know. Students have access to tools that can generate grammatically correct prose, reorganize paragraphs, adjust tone, and even imitate disciplinary conventions in a matter of seconds.
AI has pushed me toward a different question altogether. What evidence of learning do I actually want to see?
If the primary reason we ask students to explain their thinking is to prove they didn’t use AI, haven’t we simply built another surveillance mechanism into our classrooms?

But if the reason we ask students to explain their thinking is because understanding their reasoning gives us better evidence of learning, then we’ve changed what the assessment is for. The assignment may look exactly the same, but the pedagogy is completely different.
Educational research has consistently shown that metacognition—the ability to monitor and explain one’s own thinking—supports deeper learning.
the most important lesson AI has taught me is that good assessment has never been about collecting finished products. It has always been about finding meaningful evidence of learning.
